items.stem: A company sells furniture online. Its product pages load images from one Amazon S3 bucket in the us-east-1 Region, and the images change only a few times each year. The company now has users around the world. Users in Asia and Europe report that product pages load slowly because each image takes a long time to download. The company wants to reduce the time that these users wait for the images. What should a solutions architect recommend?
keywords: the images change only a few times each year
takes a long time to download

options.text: Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the edge locations near users in Asia and Europe, and copy the product images to the instances.
options.why: Edge locations run AWS services, not your instances: [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon Route 53, AWS Firewall Manager, AWS Shield, and AWS WAF services are provided through AWS Edge Locations](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-edge-location-services).

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as its origin, and load the product images through the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: The distribution caches the images at edge locations, and each user reaches the [edge location that provides the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge).

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with the S3 bucket as its endpoint, so that edge locations keep copies of the images.
options.why: Global Accelerator works by [proxying packets at the edge](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-vs-cloudfront-content-types), and its endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and load the product images through the accelerated endpoint name of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and [no data is ever saved](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-no-data-at-edge) at the edge, so each image still comes from us-east-1.
options.misconception: believes that S3 Transfer Acceleration keeps copies of files near the users, like a cache

items.explanation: The images rarely change and the users are far from us-east-1, so the fix is a cache near the users. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content), and each request goes to the [edge location that provides the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge). After the first request for an image, CloudFront [adds the object to the cache](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-first-byte-forwarded-and-cached) for the next request, so later users wait less.
items.takeaway: Static files and users far from the bucket: put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket.
items.twin: If the stem said "customers upload large videos to the bucket from many countries" instead: S3 Transfer Acceleration, because it is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use).
items.say: The images rarely change, so I'd cache them at the edge with CloudFront.

solvers.stem_only: Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket (origin access control) and load the images through the distribution, so edge locations cache the rarely changing images close to users in Asia and Europe.

items.stem: A company serves a static website from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Visitors read pages and download files, and they never upload anything. S3 Cross-Region Replication copies every object to a second bucket in us-west-2. The website must stay highly available if the us-east-1 bucket starts to return server errors during a Regional problem. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: copies every object to a second bucket in us-west-2

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the 5xx error rate of the distribution, and let the alarm start a script that changes the origin of the distribution to the us-west-2 bucket.
options.why: It works, but edits made during an outage [depend on the CloudFront control plane](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-static-stability-use-origin-failover-not-manual), and the alarm and the script are more parts to run.
options.misconception: believes that a script that edits the distribution during an outage is as dependable as failover that is configured in advance

options.text: Associate a Lambda@Edge function with the origin response event, and let the function fetch the file from the us-west-2 bucket when the us-east-1 bucket returns an error.
options.why: It works, because Lambda@Edge can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed), but it is code to write and maintain for a retry that CloudFront offers as a setting.

options.text: Create an origin group that fails over from the us-east-1 bucket to the us-west-2 bucket on 5xx status codes, and use the group in the default cache behavior.
options.why: The origin group is a setting: CloudFront lets you [assign a backup origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-origin-failover-backup-origin), and the replica bucket already holds every file.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with both buckets as endpoints, and let its health checks move the traffic to the us-west-2 bucket.
options.why: Accelerator endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, so an S3 bucket cannot be one.
options.misconception: believes that Global Accelerator can route traffic to S3 buckets

items.explanation: Origin failover is built into CloudFront. It needs [a distribution with at least two origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-needs-two-origins), an origin group, and a cache behavior that uses the group. When the primary origin fails or returns one of the chosen status codes, [CloudFront automatically switches to the secondary origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-switches-to-secondary). No person and no code acts during the outage.
items.takeaway: A replica origin behind CloudFront: use an origin group, not a script or edge code.
items.twin: If the stem said "visitors also upload files with PUT requests" instead: the uploads would not fail over, because CloudFront fails over [only when the HTTP method of the viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options) request is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS.

solvers.stem_only: Use a CloudFront origin group with the us-east-1 bucket as primary and the replicated us-west-2 bucket as secondary, failing over on 5xx status codes; read-only GET/HEAD traffic suits origin failover and needs no custom code.

items.stem: A company hosts the static assets of a web application in an Amazon S3 bucket. The API of the application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The browser sends API calls to paths that start with /api/, and every other path is a static asset. All requests must use one domain name. Static assets must be cached at edge locations, and API responses must not be cached. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: All requests must use one domain name
API responses must not be cached

options.text: Create two CloudFront distributions, one with the bucket as its origin and one with the load balancer as its origin, and give each distribution its own domain name.
options.why: It breaks the one-domain requirement, and one distribution can serve both origins, because [you specify the one origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each) in each cache behavior.
options.misconception: believes that a CloudFront distribution can use one origin, so each origin needs its own distribution

options.text: Copy the static assets to the EC2 instances, and create one CloudFront distribution with the load balancer as its origin and a /api/* behavior that uses CachingDisabled.
options.why: It works, but the instances then store, deploy and serve every asset, which is more work than keeping the bucket as a second origin.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with the bucket and the load balancer as endpoints, and send the /api/ paths to the load balancer endpoint.
options.why: Accelerator endpoints are [Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-standard-endpoint-types), EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, so the bucket cannot be one.
options.misconception: believes that Global Accelerator can route requests to S3 buckets by URL path

options.text: Create one CloudFront distribution with both origins, a /api/* cache behavior for the load balancer with CachingDisabled, and a default cache behavior for the bucket.
options.why: In each cache behavior [you specify the one origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each), and [the first match determines which cache behavior](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins) handles the path.

items.explanation: One distribution can hold both origins, because in each cache behavior [you specify the one origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-one-origin-each). CloudFront compares the path with the behaviors in order, and [the first match determines which cache behavior](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-behavior-first-match-wins) applies. The /api/* behavior uses CachingDisabled, and [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled). The default behavior serves the bucket from the edge caches.
items.takeaway: Two origins under one domain name: one distribution, with one cache behavior for each path pattern.
items.twin: If the stem said "API responses can be cached for a few seconds" instead: keep both behaviors, but give the /api/* behavior a cache policy with a short time to live (TTL) in place of CachingDisabled.

solvers.stem_only: One CloudFront distribution with two origins: the S3 bucket for the default cache behavior (cached) and the ALB for a /api/* cache behavior with caching disabled (CachingDisabled policy).

items.stem: A company runs an online course website. Each course video uses HLS, so the video is split into hundreds of small segment files that the player requests one after another. The files are served through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Only signed-in subscribers can watch, and each subscriber must get temporary access to all files of a video. The company does not want to change the URLs that the video player requests. What should the company use to control access?
keywords: temporary access to all files of a video
does not want to change the URLs

options.text: A CloudFront signed URL for each segment file, which the website creates for a subscriber after sign-in
options.why: Signed URLs fit when you [restrict access to individual files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-url-when-individual-files-or-no-cookies); hundreds of segments need hundreds of new URLs, so the URLs change.

options.text: CloudFront geographic restriction that allows the countries where the subscribers of the company live
options.why: [Geographic restrictions apply to an entire distribution](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-geo-restriction-country-level-whole-distribution) at the country level, so anyone in an allowed country can watch.
options.misconception: believes that geographic restriction can tell paying subscribers from other viewers

options.text: CloudFront signed cookies, which the website sets for a subscriber after sign-in, with an expiration time for the access
options.why: Signed cookies give [access to multiple restricted files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls) with one sign-in, and the player keeps its current URLs.

options.text: An AWS WAF web ACL on the distribution that allows the IP addresses of signed-in subscribers
options.why: Subscribers change networks and share addresses, so an IP allow list does not follow the person who paid, and it has no expiration time.
options.misconception: believes that an IP address allow list identifies individual paying users

items.explanation: Signed cookies fit two parts of the stem: they give [access to multiple restricted files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls), such as every segment of one video, and they work when [you don't want to change your current URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-cookies-when-multiple-files-or-keep-urls). The website sets an expiration time in the cookies, so the access is temporary.
items.takeaway: Many private files for one user and URLs that stay the same: CloudFront signed cookies.
items.twin: If the stem said "each subscriber downloads one PDF certificate" instead: a signed URL, because signed URLs fit when you [restrict access to individual files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signed-url-when-individual-files-or-no-cookies).

solvers.stem_only: CloudFront signed cookies set after sign-in with an expiration: they cover many files (all HLS segments) without changing the requested URLs, unlike signed URLs.

items.stem: A company runs a product catalog website on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Viewers are in many countries. The cache hit ratio is low, and the origin instances are overloaded. The cache policy of the distribution includes all query strings, all cookies and the User-Agent header in the cache key. Each catalog page changes only with the value of the lang query string. The team does not want to write or maintain any code for this change. Which combination of steps will raise the cache hit ratio and reduce the origin load with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: changes only with the value of the lang query string
does not want to write or maintain any code

options.text: Attach a cache policy to the cache behavior that includes only the lang query string in the cache key, with no cookies and no headers.
options.why: AWS says to [forward only the query string parameters](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values) that change the response.

options.text: Associate a CloudFront function with the viewer request event that removes all cookies, the User-Agent header and every query string except lang.
options.why: It works, because [cache key normalization](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases) suits CloudFront Functions, but it is code to write and maintain where a policy setting is enough.

options.text: Keep all cookies in the cache key, and add every other viewer header to it, so that each cached copy matches its request more exactly.
options.why: Every extra value splits a page into more copies; AWS says to [forward only specified cookies instead of forwarding all](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-hit-ratio-forward-only-needed-values) cookies.

options.text: Turn on Origin Shield for the origin, and choose the AWS Region that has the lowest latency to the EC2 instances of the catalog.
options.why: Origin Shield is a [centralized caching layer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-origin-shield-central-cache-layer), placed in [the AWS Region that has the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-shield-choose-lowest-latency-region) to the origin.

options.text: Create an invalidation for the /* path every hour, so that the edge locations keep a fresh copy of every catalog page.
options.why: An invalidation empties the cache, so the next requests go to the origin; AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning).
options.misconception: believes that frequent invalidations keep the cache fresh without losing cache hits

items.explanation: Values in the cache key that do not change the page split it into many separate copies. A cache policy decides what is [included in the cache key](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cache-policy-controls-cache-key), so a key with only lang raises the hit ratio. With Origin Shield, CloudFront will [route all origin fetches through Origin Shield](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-origin-shield-central-cache-layer), one more cache before the origin.
items.takeaway: Low hit ratio: shrink the cache key to the values that change the page, then add Origin Shield.
items.twin: If the stem said "every page is different for each signed-in user" instead: the pages are not cacheable, and the managed CachingDisabled policy is [useful for dynamic content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled).

solvers.stem_only: Replace the cache policy with one whose cache key holds only the lang query string (no cookies, no headers), which is configuration and not code; and turn on Origin Shield in the Region closest to the origin so that requests from the many edge locations collapse into one caching layer before the EC2 origin.

items.stem: A company runs a payments API on Amazon EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. Partner companies call the API with HTTPS POST requests. The firewalls of the partners allow outbound traffic only to IP addresses on an allow list, and the partners update their lists rarely. If the API fails in one Region, partner traffic must move automatically to another Region. Which solution will provide the FASTEST failover between the Regions?
keywords: allow outbound traffic only to IP addresses on an allow list

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with an endpoint group in each Region for the Application Load Balancer of that Region, and give its static IP addresses to the partners.
options.why: The accelerator has [two IPv4 static IP addresses](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-two-static-ipv4-independent-network-zones) for the allow list, and when a Region fails it [redirects traffic to the next optimal AWS Region](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-multi-region-failover-redirects-traffic).

options.text: Place a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of each Application Load Balancer, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks for the Network Load Balancers.
options.why: It works, but resolvers cache DNS answers [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so some partners keep calling the failed Region until the cached answer expires.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with an origin group that contains both Application Load Balancers, and fail over to the us-west-2 load balancer on 5xx status codes.
options.why: The partners send POST requests, and CloudFront fails over [only when the HTTP method of the viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-failover-only-get-head-options) request is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS.

options.text: Attach Elastic IP addresses to the Application Load Balancer in each Region, and create Amazon Route 53 weighted records with health checks that point to those addresses.
options.why: In the Elastic Load Balancing feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) is a feature of the Network Load Balancer, not of the Application Load Balancer.

items.explanation: The partners need fixed addresses, and a DNS-based failover waits for caches. With Global Accelerator you do not depend on [the IP address caching settings of client devices](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds), and [change propagation takes a matter of seconds](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds). The partners keep calling the same two addresses while traffic moves to the healthy Region.
items.takeaway: Fixed IP addresses and fast Region failover for POST traffic: AWS Global Accelerator.
items.twin: If the stem said "partners resolve a DNS name and accept several minutes of downtime" instead: DNS failover records are enough, because a wait [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control) is acceptable.
items.say: Partners allow-list addresses and send POST requests, so I'd use Global Accelerator: two fixed addresses and failover in seconds.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the FASTEST failover between the Regions.
I mark the constraints: the partners send HTTPS POST requests, their firewalls allow only listed IP addresses, and traffic must move automatically to another Region.
Before I look at the options, I predict a CloudFront distribution with an origin group, because an origin group switches to a second origin without a person.
I remove the Elastic IP addresses on the Application Load Balancers, because in the feature table only the Network Load Balancer has static or Elastic IP addresses.

Between the CloudFront origin group and Global Accelerator, the difference is the request method and the addresses. My first idea breaks because CloudFront fails over only GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests, and the partners send POST requests. The Route 53 option works, but resolvers keep old answers until their TTL runs out.
Check: Global Accelerator gives two static IP addresses for the allow list, moves traffic to the healthy Region, and does not wait for DNS caches. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Global Accelerator with an endpoint group per Region holding the ALB: two static anycast IPs for the partner allow lists, and health-check-based failover that does not depend on DNS caching; CloudFront origin failover does not apply to POST.

items.stem: A news company serves its website to millions of readers through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is a group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache. A new feature needs a small piece of logic that runs for every viewer request. Each request must be rewritten to a language folder, such as /de/, based on the Accept-Language header of the request. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache

options.text: Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: CloudFront Functions suit [URL redirects or rewrites](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases), and they cost [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).

options.text: Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: It works, but Lambda@Edge costs more for the same rewrite: CloudFront Functions cost [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).

options.text: Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the origin request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: When the page is in the cache, [the function doesn't execute](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-origin-request-only-on-miss), so cached pages skip the rewrite and readers get another language.
options.misconception: believes that an origin request function runs for every viewer request, cache hits included

options.text: Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the default cache behavior, and add the logic to the application that runs on the EC2 instances.
options.why: It works, but [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled), so every request reaches the EC2 instances, which costs far more than a rewrite at the edge.

items.explanation: A URL rewrite is light work that needs no network call, and CloudFront Functions suit [URL redirects or rewrites](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases). The function rewrites the path at the edge on the viewer request, so each language folder gets its own cached copy. CloudFront Functions cost [a fraction of the price of AWS Lambda@Edge](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-functions-cheaper-than-lambda-edge).
items.takeaway: Light URL or header work on every request: a CloudFront function on the viewer request event.
items.twin: If the stem said "Each request must be checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table" instead: a Lambda@Edge function, because it can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed).
items.say: A path rewrite is light work, so a CloudFront function on the viewer request is the cheapest choice.

solvers.stem_only: A CloudFront Functions function on the viewer request event: lightweight header-based URL rewrite on every request, cheapest option at high volume; Lambda@Edge is more expensive and not needed.

items.stem: A company runs a single-page web application from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The team deploys new JavaScript and CSS files several times each day under the same file names. After each deployment, some users keep running the old files, including users whose browser or corporate proxy kept a copy. The team creates invalidations for the changed files after each deployment, and the invalidation charges grow every month. Users must get the new files right after each deployment. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: browser or corporate proxy kept a copy

options.text: Keep the current file names, and create one invalidation for the /* path after each deployment, because a wildcard path counts as one invalidation path.
options.why: The wildcard [counts as one path](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-invalidation-wildcard-counts-one-path), but invalidation clears the CloudFront caches, not the copies that browsers and corporate proxies keep.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning for the origin bucket, so that each deployment stores a new object version that CloudFront serves to users after the upload.
options.why: CloudFront file versioning [is not related to Amazon S3 object versioning](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-versioning-not-s3-versioning); the file names stay the same, so cached copies stay old.
options.misconception: believes that S3 object versioning makes CloudFront and browsers fetch the newest file

options.text: Add a version identifier to the JavaScript and CSS file names in each deployment, give index.html a short TTL, and give the versioned files a long TTL.
options.why: New names reach every user, also through browser and proxy copies, and [versioning is less expensive](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-invalidation-prefer-versioning-for-frequent-updates) than invalidation.

options.text: Set a Cache-Control max-age of 0 seconds on every file in the bucket, so that CloudFront, browsers and proxies revalidate each file with the origin on every request.
options.why: It works, but with [0 seconds](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-expiration-zero-seconds-revalidates) CloudFront will [revalidate every request with the origin server](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-expiration-zero-seconds-revalidates), so every page load pays for origin requests.

items.explanation: Old copies live in edge caches, browsers and corporate proxies. A new file name is a new URL, so every cache fetches the new file, and index.html with a short TTL points to it. AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning) and to [implement a versioning system for your files](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning).
items.takeaway: Frequent releases behind CloudFront: change the file names, not the cache.
items.twin: If the stem said "a file with wrong prices must disappear from the edge caches now" instead: create an invalidation, because AWS says to [use invalidation only in unexpected circumstances](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-invalidate-only-unexpected-use-versioning) like this one.
items.say: Version the file names: every cache sees a new URL, and you stop paying for invalidations.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to give users the new files right after each deployment.
I mark the constraints: the file names stay the same, browsers and corporate proxies keep copies, the invalidation charges grow, and users need the new files right after each deployment.
Before I look at the options, I predict versioned file names, because a new name is a new URL that no cache holds yet.
I remove the /* invalidation, because it clears the CloudFront caches but not the browsers or the proxies. I remove S3 Versioning, because it is not related to CloudFront file versioning.
Between versioned names and a max-age of 0 seconds, the difference is the number of origin requests; the stem asks for the lowest cost, so revalidating every request loses.
Check: versioned names reach browsers, proxies and edge caches, need no invalidation, and keep long TTLs for the files. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Cache busting: put a version or content hash in the JS/CSS file names on each deployment with long TTLs, and give index.html a short TTL so it points to the new names; no invalidations needed and browser/proxy copies are bypassed.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is internet-facing in public subnets. An Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the load balancer caches static pages at edge locations near users. A security review requires that the load balancer is no longer internet-facing and that users reach the application only through CloudFront. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the internet-facing load balancer in the public subnets, and allow inbound traffic in its security group only from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront.
options.why: The security group blocks other callers, but the load balancer stays internet-facing, which the security review forbids.

options.text: Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets for the instances, and add the internal load balancer to the distribution as a VPC origin.
options.why: CloudFront can use [internal Application Load Balancers inside private subnets](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-internal-needs-vpc-origins) through VPC origins, [making CloudFront the single point of entry](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpc-origin-cloudfront-single-entry-point).

options.text: Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, and run proxy instances in public subnets that accept traffic from CloudFront and forward it to the load balancer.
options.why: It works, but the proxy instances are more servers to patch, scale and protect; a VPC origin reaches the load balancer [over a private, secure connection](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpc-origin-cloudfront-single-entry-point).

options.text: Keep the current load balancer as the origin, and attach origin access control to the load balancer origin so that it accepts signed CloudFront requests.
options.why: Origin access control restricts [Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) Origins, AWS Elemental Origins, and Lambda Function URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and a load balancer is not one of them.
options.misconception: believes that origin access control can protect any origin, such as a load balancer

items.explanation: VPC origins let CloudFront use an [Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer, or EC2 instance in a private subnet](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-private-subnet-vpc-origin). The internal load balancer has no internet entry point, and CloudFront becomes the one way in. Static pages still come from the edge caches, so caching does not change.
items.takeaway: A private load balancer behind CloudFront: make it internal and add it as a VPC origin.
items.twin: If the stem said "the load balancer must stay internet-facing until next quarter" instead: limit its security group to the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), so that other callers are blocked.

solvers.stem_only: Use CloudFront VPC origins: move to an internal ALB in private subnets and add it as a VPC origin, so the ALB is no longer internet-facing and only CloudFront can reach it.

items.stem: A company distributes installers for its desktop software from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. Users around the world download the installers directly from the bucket, and each new version is downloaded millions of times in its first week. Users far from us-east-1 report slow downloads, and the data transfer charges of the bucket keep growing. The company must reduce download times and keep data transfer costs low. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

options.text: Replicate the bucket to S3 buckets in Europe and Asia with S3 Cross-Region Replication, and send each user to the nearest bucket instead of paying CloudFront transfer charges.
options.why: Each regional bucket still serves every download without a cache, and the copies add storage and replication charges, while the fetch from S3 to CloudFront is [always free when using AWS origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).

options.text: Move the installers to Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer, and put an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator in front of the load balancer.
options.why: It works for speed, but an accelerator adds [a fixed hourly fee](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-price-fixed-hourly-fee-plus-dt-premium) and a [Data Transfer-Premium fee (DT-Premium)](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-price-fixed-hourly-fee-plus-dt-premium), and nothing is cached.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket, and change the download links to use the accelerated endpoint name of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration is for customers who [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and [no data is ever saved](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-no-data-at-edge) at the edge, so every download still leaves the bucket.
options.misconception: believes that S3 Transfer Acceleration caches popular downloads at edge locations

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin, and change the download links to use the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: Edge caches serve the repeated downloads, and transfer from S3 to CloudFront is [always free when using AWS origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).

items.explanation: Each installer is downloaded millions of times, so edge caches can answer most downloads. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content). Amazon S3 does not charge for [data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront](../facts/s3.md#s3-pricing-data-transfer-to-cloudfront-free), and the company pays for [the outbound data transfer from CloudFront](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins) to the users.
items.takeaway: Popular downloads for users far away: CloudFront in front of the bucket is faster, and the origin fetch is free.
items.twin: If the stem said "the installers are served by EC2 instances behind a load balancer" instead: CloudFront still fits, because transfer from Elastic Load Balancing is also [always free when using AWS origins](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-price-origin-to-cloudfront-always-free-aws-origins).
items.say: Put CloudFront in front of the bucket: repeat downloads come from the edge, and S3 to CloudFront transfer is free.

solvers.stem_only: Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket and use its domain in the download links: edge caching serves the millions of repeat downloads, S3-to-CloudFront transfer is free and CloudFront data transfer out costs less than S3 direct.

items.stem: A news company serves its website to millions of readers through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is a group of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache. A new feature needs a small piece of logic that runs for every viewer request. Each request must be checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and blocked readers must get an error page. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: checked against a list of blocked reader accounts in an Amazon DynamoDB table
Most page requests are served from the CloudFront cache

options.text: Write the logic as a CloudFront function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: CloudFront Functions have no [network access](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access), so the function cannot read the list in the DynamoDB table.

options.text: Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the viewer request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: Lambda@Edge can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed), and a viewer request trigger runs [before it checks to see whether the requested](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-viewer-request-before-cache) object is in the cache.

options.text: Write the logic as a Lambda@Edge function, and associate the function with the origin request event of the default cache behavior of the distribution.
options.why: When the page is in the cache, [the function doesn't execute](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-origin-request-only-on-miss), so blocked readers still get cached pages.
options.misconception: believes that an origin request function runs for every viewer request, cache hits included

options.text: Attach the managed CachingDisabled cache policy to the default cache behavior, and add the logic to the application that runs on the EC2 instances.
options.why: It works, but [this policy disables caching](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-managed-policy-caching-disabled), so every request reaches the EC2 instances, which costs far more than a check at the edge.

items.explanation: The check needs a call to DynamoDB on every request, cached pages included. Lambda@Edge can [make network calls to external resources](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-network-calls-allowed), and a viewer request trigger runs [when CloudFront receives a request from a viewer](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-lambda-edge-viewer-request-before-cache), before the cache check. CloudFront Functions are cheaper, but they have no [network access](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-no-network-no-body-fs-access).
items.takeaway: Edge logic that calls another service on every request: Lambda@Edge on the viewer request event.
items.twin: If the stem said "Each request must be rewritten to a language folder, such as /de/, based on the Accept-Language header of the request" instead: a CloudFront function, because it suits [URL redirects or rewrites](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-functions-use-cases).

solvers.stem_only: Lambda@Edge on the viewer request event, because the check must run on every request (including cache hits) and must call DynamoDB over the network, which CloudFront Functions cannot do; origin request would run only on cache misses.

items.stem: A gaming company runs game servers on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Players worldwide connect to these servers, many of them through partner networks. Players send their moves over UDP, and partner networks must allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses. The company wants to improve response times for players who are far from both Regions. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for players?
keywords: allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the two Network Load Balancers as origins, and point the game client at the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: CloudFront carries [content that can be sent using the HTTP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-content-types-http-websocket) or WebSocket protocols, so it is the wrong service for the UDP game moves.
options.misconception: CloudFront can accelerate any traffic, including UDP game traffic

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one listener and an endpoint group for the Network Load Balancer in each of the two Regions.
options.why: The accelerator supports [both TCP and UDP protocols](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-protocols-tcp-and-udp), and its static addresses [accept incoming traffic onto the AWS global network](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-edge-location-then-global-network) at the edge location closest to each player.

options.text: Create Amazon Route 53 latency-based records that point to the two Network Load Balancers, and point the game client at the name of the records.
options.why: It works, but Route 53 only answers DNS queries with the record whose [Region gives the user the lowest latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-routing-lowest-latency-region); the game packets do not enter AWS at an edge location.

options.text: Turn on Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for a bucket that stores the game data, and point the game client at the accelerated endpoint of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration helps clients that [upload to a centralized general purpose bucket](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-when-to-use), and the game moves go to the instances, not to a bucket.
options.misconception: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up any application traffic

items.explanation: UDP traffic and a fixed set of addresses point to Global Accelerator, a fit for [gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), or Voice over IP](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-good-fit-non-http-static-ip-fast-failover). It gives [two IPv4 static IP addresses](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-two-static-ipv4-independent-network-zones) for the allow lists and [routes traffic to the closest edge location](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-anycast-nearest-edge-then-closest-endpoint), then over the AWS network to the closest Regional endpoint.
items.takeaway: UDP traffic or fixed IP addresses: Global Accelerator. Cacheable HTTP content: CloudFront.
items.twin: If the stem said "Players download large game patch files over HTTPS, and the files change once a week" instead: the CloudFront distribution, because CloudFront [adds the object to the cache](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-first-byte-forwarded-and-cached) for the next request.
items.say: UDP plus fixed addresses means Global Accelerator; CloudFront is for HTTP content that it can cache.

solvers.stem_only: AWS Global Accelerator in front of the two NLBs (endpoint group per Region): supports UDP, gives two static anycast IPs for allow lists, and carries traffic over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge.

items.stem: A company serves an online store at shop.example.com through an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin is an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in eu-central-1, and the distribution reaches it at origin.example.com. The viewer protocol policy redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and the distribution uses an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for shop.example.com. A security review finds that the load balancer has only an HTTP listener. The company must ensure that data is encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the load balancer has only an HTTP listener
encrypted in transit all the way to the load balancer

options.text: Change the viewer protocol policy to HTTPS Only, so that CloudFront refuses HTTP requests from viewers and keeps each request encrypted on its way to the load balancer.
options.why: The two legs are separate settings: CloudFront serves objects [regardless of whether the protocol used](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-https-viewer-origin-protocol-independent) toward the origin matches the viewer's, so the origin leg stays HTTP.

options.text: Configure field-level encryption for the form fields that hold customer data, so that CloudFront encrypts those fields before it forwards each request to the load balancer.
options.why: Field-level encryption [adds an additional layer of security](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-fle-layer-on-https-selected-fields) for chosen fields on top of HTTPS; the rest of each request still crosses the origin leg over HTTP.
options.misconception: field-level encryption encrypts the whole connection to the origin

options.text: Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer that passes TCP port 443 to the instances, and install a certificate from a third-party authority on each instance.
options.why: It works, but it replaces the load balancer and puts third-party certificates on every instance, while for ACM certificates [ACM manages certificate renewals for you](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-acm-managed-renewal).

options.text: Request an ACM certificate for origin.example.com in eu-central-1, add an HTTPS listener with it to the load balancer, and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.
options.why: With the origin policy HTTPS only, [CloudFront uses only HTTPS to access the origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-origin-protocol-https-only), and the certificate name [must match the domain name that you specify](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-https-origin-domain-must-match) as the origin.

items.explanation: Encryption in transit through CloudFront has two settings: [require that viewers use HTTPS](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https), which the redirect already does, and [use HTTPS to get files from your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-encrypt-in-transit-viewer-and-origin-https). The load balancer needs an HTTPS listener whose ACM certificate [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.
items.takeaway: CloudFront encrypts two legs with two settings: the viewer protocol policy and the origin protocol policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "the viewer protocol policy allows HTTP and HTTPS" instead: also set it to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, because then [HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-vpp-redirect-http-to-https).
items.say: The viewer side is already HTTPS. I add an HTTPS listener on the load balancer and set the origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

solvers.stem_only: Add an HTTPS listener to the ALB with an ACM certificate for origin.example.com requested in the ALB's Region (eu-central-1), and set the CloudFront origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

items.stem: A company runs a banking API behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin returns account balances with the header Cache-Control: no-cache. The /api/* cache behavior uses a custom cache policy, created by a former team member, with a Minimum TTL of 3600 seconds. After a payment, users see their old balance for up to an hour. Each balance request must return the current balance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep the cache policy as it is, and change the origin so that each balance response also carries the Cache-Control directives no-store and private.
options.why: CloudFront keeps the Minimum TTL even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), so more directives change nothing while the floor stays.
options.misconception: a stronger Cache-Control directive from the origin beats the Minimum TTL

options.text: Change the mobile and web clients to add a unique query string value to each balance request, and include all query strings in the cache key.
options.why: It works, because every request gets its own cache key, but it changes every client and fills the cache with single-use copies.

options.text: Edit the custom cache policy of the /api/* cache behavior, and set its Minimum TTL to 0 seconds so that the origin's headers decide caching.
options.why: The floor is the fault: when the [minimum TTL is greater than 0](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), CloudFront ignores no-cache for that long. At 0, the header of the origin decides again.

options.text: Change the mobile and web clients to send the header Cache-Control: no-cache with each balance request, so that CloudFront fetches a fresh copy from the origin.
options.why: [CloudFront ignores those header fields in viewer requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-expiration-viewer-cache-control-ignored), so a viewer cannot force a trip to the origin while the cached copy is still valid.
options.misconception: a viewer can force CloudFront to skip its cache

items.explanation: The origin already sends no-cache, but the cache policy sets a floor. If the [minimum TTL is greater than 0](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache), CloudFront caches for at least that time, even when the origin sends no-cache, [no-store, or private](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-min-ttl-above-zero-overrides-no-cache). A Minimum TTL of 0 removes the floor with one change in the policy.
items.takeaway: Stale content although the origin says no-cache: check the Minimum TTL of the cache policy first.
items.twin: If the stem said "the origin sends no Cache-Control header, and the Default TTL is 3600 seconds" instead: lower the Default TTL, because CloudFront uses it [as the object's TTL](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-ttl-default-ttl-only-without-headers) when no such header arrives.
items.say: A Minimum TTL above zero beats no-cache, so I set the Minimum TTL of that policy to zero.

solvers.stem_only: A Minimum TTL above 0 overrides the origin's Cache-Control no-cache/no-store/private; set the cache policy's Minimum TTL to 0 (or use CachingDisabled) for /api/* so the origin headers decide.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is the origin of an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Attackers now send requests to the DNS name of the load balancer directly, which bypasses the protections at CloudFront. The load balancer must stay internet-facing until a network redesign next quarter. The load balancer must not accept connections from IP addresses outside CloudFront, and only requests that come through the company's own distribution may reach the application. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must not accept connections from IP addresses outside CloudFront
only requests that come through the company's own distribution

options.text: Configure origin access control on the load balancer origin, so that CloudFront signs each request and the load balancer rejects every request without a signature.
options.why: Origin access control covers Amazon Simple Storage Service ([S3) Origins, AWS Elemental Origins, and Lambda Function URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and a load balancer is not one of them.
options.misconception: origin access control works for any origin type

options.text: In the security group of the load balancer, allow inbound HTTPS from the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront, and remove the other inbound rules.
options.why: The group then admits only the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), which [prevents non-CloudFront traffic from reaching your origin](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers).

options.text: Add a deny rule to the network ACL of the load balancer subnets for each IP address that sends requests directly to the load balancer.
options.why: A deny list blocks known addresses, and [you can't reference prefix lists in network ACL rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-no-prefix-lists), so a network ACL cannot admit CloudFront alone.

options.text: Configure CloudFront to add a secret custom header to origin requests, and add a listener rule that forwards only the requests that carry that header.
options.why: CloudFront can [add a custom HTTP header to requests](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https), and the listener can [only forward requests that contain the custom HTTP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-restrict-custom-header-and-https) header that marks this distribution.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function each day that reads the published CloudFront IP ranges and rewrites the inbound rules of the security group of the load balancer.
options.why: It works, but it is code to run and fix, while [the CloudFront managed prefix list contains the IP](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-prefix-list-origin-facing-servers) ranges already and stays current.

items.explanation: Two locks work together on an internet-facing origin. The security group allows the [AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg), and AWS says to [remove any other inbound rules](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cloudfront-prefix-list-sg). A secret header that CloudFront adds marks the requests of this distribution.
items.takeaway: Public load balancer behind CloudFront: prefix list in the security group plus a secret header. Private load balancer: VPC origin.
items.twin: If the stem said "the load balancer can move to private subnets now" instead: use a VPC origin, because CloudFront works with [internal Application Load Balancers inside private subnets](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-alb-internal-needs-vpc-origins).
items.say: While the load balancer stays public, I allow only the CloudFront prefix list and check a secret header from CloudFront.

solvers.stem_only: Restrict the ALB security group to the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing addresses (no IP-range maintenance), and have CloudFront add a secret custom origin header that an ALB listener rule requires (forward only when the header matches, default action returns 403), so that other customers' distributions cannot reach the application.

items.stem: A company runs a TCP application on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer in us-east-1. A standby copy runs behind a second Network Load Balancer in a second Region, us-west-2. An AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator has one listener with an endpoint group for the us-east-1 load balancer. During normal operation, all traffic must go to us-east-1. If the us-east-1 endpoints become unhealthy, traffic must move to us-west-2 automatically. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: all traffic must go to us-east-1

options.text: Register the us-west-2 Network Load Balancer as a second endpoint in the us-east-1 endpoint group, and set the weight of that endpoint to 0.
options.why: You associate [each endpoint group with one AWS Region](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region), so the us-east-1 group cannot hold a load balancer from us-west-2.
options.misconception: one endpoint group can hold endpoints from more than one Region

options.text: Add an endpoint group for us-west-2 to the existing listener, and register the us-west-2 Network Load Balancer in that endpoint group as an endpoint.
options.why: You [associate each listener with one or more endpoint](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region) groups and [each endpoint group with one AWS Region](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-listener-endpoint-group-per-region), so us-west-2 needs its own group.

options.text: Create a second accelerator for the us-west-2 load balancer, and create Amazon Route 53 failover records with health checks that point to the two accelerators.
options.why: It works, but it adds an accelerator and DNS records, while one accelerator does not depend on [the IP address caching settings of client devices](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-no-dns-cache-dependency-seconds).

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-west-2 endpoint group to 0 percent, and keep the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group at 100 percent.
options.why: A dial at 0 keeps us-west-2 out of normal traffic, and in a failover [Global Accelerator ignores the traffic dial setting](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial).

options.text: Set the client affinity of the listener to Source IP, so that each client keeps using the us-east-1 endpoints while those endpoints stay healthy.
options.why: Client affinity can [direct all requests from a user](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-client-affinity-for-stateful-apps) to the same endpoint for stateful applications; it does not choose an active Region.
options.misconception: client affinity decides which Region is active

items.explanation: The traffic dial supports [active-active and active-standby setups](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-weights-active-active-standby). The standby group's dial is 0, so it gets no normal traffic; when us-east-1 has no healthy endpoint, [Global Accelerator ignores the traffic dial setting](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-failover-to-another-endpoint-group-ignores-dial) and fails over.
items.takeaway: Active-standby in Global Accelerator: the standby endpoint group gets a traffic dial of 0, and failover ignores the dial.
items.twin: If the stem said "each Region must serve the users closest to it" instead: keep both traffic dials at their default of [100%](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-traffic-dial-default-100-percent) after you add the second endpoint group.
items.say: I add a us-west-2 endpoint group with its dial at zero; failover ignores the dial, so it is a standby.

solvers.stem_only: Add a second endpoint group for us-west-2 on the same listener with the us-west-2 NLB as its endpoint, and set that group's traffic dial to 0 percent (us-east-1 at 100 percent); Global Accelerator health checks then fail traffic over to the us-west-2 group only when the us-east-1 endpoints are unhealthy.

items.stem: A company runs a photo-sharing mobile app. Users upload photos with HTTP PUT requests through an Amazon CloudFront distribution to an Amazon S3 bucket, and other users download the photos through the same distribution. The objects in the bucket are encrypted with server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS). The bucket must not be publicly accessible, and users must not reach the bucket directly. The company wants to restrict bucket access to the distribution. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: upload photos with HTTP PUT requests through an Amazon CloudFront distribution
encrypted with server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)

options.text: Configure an origin access identity (OAI) on the S3 origin, allow PUT in the cache behavior, and let the bucket policy and the AWS KMS key policy allow access by the OAI.
options.why: With SSE-KMS, [you must use OAC instead](../facts/s3.md#s3-website-sse-kms-needs-cloudfront-oac) of OAI, and OAI does not support [Dynamic requests (PUT, POST, or DELETE) to Amazon S3](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oai-legacy-not-for-all-scenarios), so the uploads through CloudFront fail.

options.text: Make the bucket policy allow public reads and writes, and change the app so that it sends every upload and download to the CloudFront domain name.
options.why: A public policy breaks the first requirement, and CloudFront needs none: with origin access control the bucket allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).

options.text: Send uploads to an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda function that writes each photo to the bucket, and use origin access control for downloads.
options.why: It works, but it adds an API, a function and code for every upload, while origin access control lets CloudFront send the PUT requests to the bucket itself.

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, allow PUT in the cache behavior, and let the bucket policy and the AWS KMS key policy allow access by the distribution.
options.why: Origin access control supports [Dynamic requests (PUT and DELETE) to Amazon S3](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-supports-all-regions-dynamic-requests), and for SSE-KMS [you must use OAC instead](../facts/s3.md#s3-website-sse-kms-needs-cloudfront-oac) of OAI.

items.explanation: CloudFront reaches a private S3 origin through [origin access control (OAC) and origin access identity](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-oai-two-ways-oac-recommended) (OAI), and two needs decide between them: [OAI doesn't support these features](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-supports-all-regions-dynamic-requests), such as PUT requests, and with SSE-KMS [you must use OAC instead](../facts/s3.md#s3-website-sse-kms-needs-cloudfront-oac). The bucket policy allows CloudFront [only when the request is on behalf](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) of the distribution, so the bucket stays private.
items.takeaway: For PUT requests or SSE-KMS through CloudFront to a private bucket, choose origin access control over OAI.
items.twin: If the stem said "users only download photos through the distribution" instead: still origin access control, the method that AWS recommends over the older origin access identity.
items.say: Uploads and SSE-KMS through CloudFront need origin access control, because the older OAI handles neither.

solvers.stem_only: Use origin access control (OAC) on the S3 origin, allow PUT and the other methods in the cache behavior, and grant the CloudFront service principal (conditioned on the distribution ARN) access in the bucket policy and kms:Decrypt/Encrypt/GenerateDataKey in the KMS key policy; OAI does not support SSE-KMS, and the bucket stays private with Block Public Access on.

items.stem: A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Every visitor of the website can download the files, but nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Every visitor of the website can download the files
nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
options.why: The bucket policy allows the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) for this distribution, so viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).

options.text: Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
options.why: Signed URLs check users, which the stem does not need, and they leave S3 URLs working; locking the bucket is a separate step: [this prevents someone from bypassing CloudFront](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
options.misconception: signed URLs also stop direct access to the bucket

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
options.why: A public read policy makes S3 URLs work for anyone who sends that header, and CloudFront needs no public access: the policy can allow the [CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal).

options.text: Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.
options.why: It works, but the company then runs and scales instances for every download, while origin access control is one setting plus a bucket policy.

items.explanation: The stem restricts the path, not the users: every visitor can download. With origin access control, the bucket policy allows CloudFront [only when the request is on behalf](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-oac-bucket-policy-cloudfront-service-principal) of this distribution, so the bucket stays private.
items.takeaway: Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.
items.twin: If the stem said "Only customers who paid for a course can download its files, for a limited time" instead: CloudFront signed URLs, because they serve [users who have paid a fee](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users).
items.say: Every visitor can download, so I don't check users. I lock the bucket to the distribution with origin access control.

solvers.stem_only: Origin access control on the S3 origin plus a bucket policy that allows only the CloudFront service principal with the distribution ARN as source; no signed URLs, since every visitor may download.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in ap-southeast-2. The company adds an Amazon CloudFront distribution for www.example.com in front of the load balancer. Both connections, from viewers to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the load balancer, must use HTTPS so that data stays encrypted in transit. Both must use public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), and the load balancer will use a certificate for origin.example.com. Where should the company request the two certificates?

options.text: Request both certificates in ap-southeast-2, where the application runs, and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
options.why: The distribution reads its certificate from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), whatever the Region of the origin, so a certificate in ap-southeast-2 does not appear in the distribution.

options.text: Request both certificates in US East (N. Virginia), and select each certificate in the distribution and in the load balancer.
options.why: [Certificates in ACM are regional resources](../facts/acm.md#acm-certificates-regional), so the load balancer in ap-southeast-2 cannot use a certificate from US East (N. Virginia).
options.misconception: every certificate that works with CloudFront belongs in US East (N. Virginia)

options.text: Request the www.example.com certificate in US East (N. Virginia) for the distribution, and the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.
options.why: CloudFront reads its certificate from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), and the certificate of the load balancer [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the load balancer.

options.text: Use the default CloudFront certificate for www.example.com, and request the origin.example.com certificate in ap-southeast-2 for the load balancer.
options.why: For a name such as www.example.com, [the certificate must cover the alternate domain name](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-cert-alternate-domain-covered-by-san), so the distribution needs its own certificate for that name.
options.misconception: the default CloudFront certificate covers a custom domain name

items.explanation: ACM certificates [must be in the same Region](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource) as the resource that uses them, and [the only exception is Amazon CloudFront](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-certificate-same-region-as-resource). So the certificate of the load balancer comes from ap-southeast-2, and the certificate of the distribution from [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1), from where it is [distributed to all the geographic locations](../facts/acm.md#acm-cloudfront-us-east-1).
items.takeaway: A CloudFront certificate comes from US East (N. Virginia); a load balancer certificate comes from the Region of the load balancer.
items.twin: If the stem said "a certificate from a third-party authority for www.example.com" instead: import it into ACM in US East (N. Virginia), because the rule covers all certificates, [including the certificates that you import](../facts/acm.md#acm-imported-regional-cloudfront).
items.say: CloudFront takes its certificate from us-east-1, and the load balancer takes one from its own Region.

solvers.stem_only: CloudFront requires its viewer certificate in ACM in us-east-1 (N. Virginia); the ALB requires its certificate in its own Region, ap-southeast-2.

items.stem: A company runs an online service on Amazon EC2 instances behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and us-west-2. An AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator has an endpoint group for each Region, and us-west-2 has enough capacity for all users. Users reach the service through a Route 53 alias record for the accelerator. The operations team must apply an operating system patch to the us-east-1 instances, and the patch restarts each instance. The patching must cause minimal downtime for users. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Change the Route 53 record of the service from the accelerator to the us-west-2 load balancer, wait one minute, patch the instances, and change the record back.
options.why: Resolvers cache the old answer [according to their time to live (TTL)](../facts/route53.md#route53-faq-resolver-caches-by-ttl-outside-control), so some users still reach us-east-1 through the accelerator while the instances restart.

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, wait until the existing connections close, patch the instances, and set the dial back to 100.
options.why: After a dial change, [the updated setting applies to only new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only), so the team waits for open connections to finish before the restarts.

options.text: Set the traffic dial of the us-east-1 endpoint group to 0, patch the instances right away because open connections move to us-west-2, and then set the dial back.
options.why: Open connections do not move: Global Accelerator [continues to direct traffic for established connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-established-connections-until-idle-timeout) to us-east-1, so the restarts break them.

options.text: Launch a patched fleet behind a new load balancer in us-east-1, add it to the endpoint group, and remove the old load balancer after its connections close.
options.why: It works, but it builds a new fleet and load balancer for one patch, while a traffic dial moves new connections to us-west-2 with no new resources.

items.explanation: AWS describes this maintenance step: [set the traffic dial to 0](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) for the Region, then [adjust the traffic dial to 100](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-dec-traffic-dial-zero-cuts-off-region) when the work is done. Because [the updated setting applies to only new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-traffic-dial-new-connections-only), the team waits for open connections to close before the instances restart.
items.takeaway: Planned work in one Region: turn its traffic dial down, let open connections finish, then patch.
items.twin: If the stem said "us-east-1 fails without warning" instead: health checks act without a dial change, because Global Accelerator [instantly begins directing traffic for all new connections](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-health-checks-standard-failover-new-connections) to another endpoint.
items.say: I turn the us-east-1 dial to zero, let open connections finish, patch, and turn it back up.

solvers.stem_only: Set the us-east-1 endpoint group traffic dial to 0% so new connections go to us-west-2, let existing connections drain, patch, then set the dial back to 100%.
