items.stem: A gaming company runs game servers on Amazon EC2 instances behind Network Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Players worldwide connect to these servers. The same instances also serve large game patch files to players over HTTPS through the load balancers. Every player downloads the same files, and the files change once a week. The company wants to reduce the download time of the patch files for players who are far from both Regions. Which solution will provide the LOWEST latency for these downloads?
keywords: serve large game patch files to players over HTTPS
the files change once a week

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the two Network Load Balancers as origins, and point the game client at the domain name of the distribution.
options.why: Patch files are content that [benefits from edge delivery](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content): edge locations keep copies, so most downloads are answered close to the players.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator with one listener and an endpoint group for the Network Load Balancer in each of the two Regions.
options.why: It works for HTTPS, but it improves performance by [proxying packets at the edge](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-vs-cloudfront-content-types), so every download still reaches the instances and nothing is cached.

options.text: Create Amazon Route 53 latency-based records that point to the two Network Load Balancers, and point the game client at the name of the records.
options.why: It works, but Route 53 only answers with the record whose [Region gives the user the lowest latency](../facts/route53.md#route53-latency-routing-lowest-latency-region); every download still comes from the instances in that Region.

options.text: Turn on Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for a bucket that stores the game data, and point the game client at the accelerated endpoint of the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration routes data to and from a bucket [over an optimized network path](../facts/s3.md#s3-transfer-acceleration-how-it-works), and it keeps no cached copies near the players.
options.misconception: S3 Transfer Acceleration caches content at edge locations

items.explanation: Patch files change once a week, so copies can stay at the edge. CloudFront suits [frequently accessed static content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-good-for-static-edge-content) such as software downloads. Each request goes to the [edge location that provides the lowest latency](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-request-routed-lowest-latency-edge), where a cached copy answers it without a trip to either Region.
items.takeaway: Large files that many users download: CloudFront caches them at the edge; Global Accelerator does not cache.
items.twin: If the stem said "Players send their moves over UDP, and partner networks must allow-list a fixed set of IP addresses" instead: Global Accelerator, because it supports [both TCP and UDP protocols](../facts/global-accelerator.md#global-accelerator-faq-protocols-tcp-and-udp) from fixed addresses.
items.say: Patch files are cacheable, so CloudFront serves them from edge locations near the players.

solvers.stem_only: The patch files are static, identical for all players and change weekly, so cache them at the edge: put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the existing load balancers (or an S3 origin) so far-away players download from a nearby edge location; Global Accelerator only speeds the network path and still serves every byte from the Region.

items.stem: A company sells online courses. It stores the course files in an Amazon S3 bucket and delivers them to learners through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in the same AWS account. A solutions architect must restrict access to the course files. Only customers who paid for a course can download its files, for a limited time. The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution through origin access control. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Only customers who paid for a course
The bucket already accepts reads only from the distribution

options.text: Configure origin access control on the S3 origin, and add a bucket policy that allows the CloudFront service principal to read objects for this distribution only.
options.why: Origin access control is already in place; it makes sure that [only CloudFront can access the content](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-faq-secure-origin-oac-supported-origins), and it does not know which customers paid.
options.misconception: origin access control decides which users can download

options.text: Add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application create a CloudFront signed URL for each file after the user signs in.
options.why: Signed URLs serve [users who have paid a fee](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users), and each URL carries [an ending date and time](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-url-expiry-restrictions) after which it stops working.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that allows public reads of the objects for requests that carry the domain name of the website in the Referer header.
options.why: A public read policy undoes origin access control: anyone who sends that header can then use S3 URLs, whether the person paid or not.

options.text: Serve the files through an application on Amazon EC2 instances that checks each request and reads the objects from the bucket with an IAM role.
options.why: It works, because the application can check each payment, but the company then runs a fleet for downloads that CloudFront can check at the edge.

items.explanation: The bucket is already private, so the open need is per user and per time. CloudFront restricts content to selected users by [using signed URLs or signed cookies](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-dec-signed-urls-cookies-for-paying-users). The application signs each URL after sign-in with [a trusted key group that you create](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-signer-key-group-recommended), and CloudFront checks the signature before it serves the file.
items.takeaway: Stop S3 URLs with origin access control; choose which users get files with signed URLs or signed cookies.
items.twin: If the stem said "Every visitor of the website can download the files, but nobody can download them with Amazon S3 URLs" instead: origin access control, because then viewers [cannot access it directly by using Amazon S3 URLs](../facts/cloudfront.md#cloudfront-private-s3-oac-plus-signed-urls).
items.say: The bucket is already locked to the distribution. Paying users get signed URLs that expire.

solvers.stem_only: Keep OAC, add a trusted key group to the cache behavior, and have the application issue a short-lived CloudFront signed URL for each file after it confirms the payment.
